candidates.attacker_control: The request URI (path info is percent-decoded by the servlet container, so quotes/angle brackets/spaces can be smuggled through encoded path segments) and, secondarily, the Host header used to derive the base/endpoint URLs. No authentication or application code is required; the attack is a crafted GET to the CXFServlet mount point.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the service-list branch requires either empty/"/" pathInfo or a raw request URI ending with the default "/services" or "/services/"; verified a crafted URI can satisfy this while carrying the payload in an earlier path segment (raw getRequestURI keeps the encoded characters, decoded getPathInfo carries them into the page). Verified the formatted writer is the default (?formatted=false switches to a different writer), that serviceListStyleSheet is null by default so the request-derived branch is used, and that DestinationRegistryImpl.getDestinationForPath is exact-match so ordinary service paths do not intercept the crafted URI. Also noted constraints: if a JAX-RS destination is published at "/" (prefix match via checkRestfulRequest) the request is routed to it instead; some containers/proxies may reject or normalize the encoded characters; hiding the service list (hide-service-list-page=true) removes reachability.
candidates.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting on the service-list origin under default CXF servlet settings: script execution in the context of the CXF application (session/cookie theft, request forgery against same-origin endpoints, phishing/UI redressing). The same writer additionally reflects configuration/Host-derived base addresses without encoding, but the path-info vector is directly attacker-controlled.
candidates.prerequisites: A CXF servlet-transport deployment with the default service-list page enabled (ServletController.isHideServiceList defaults to false; serviceListRelativePath defaults to "/services") mounted e.g. at /services/*, and no destination matching the crafted path (or a non-matching REST destination) so that the service-list branch is taken. Container must accept and decode encoded <, >, ", space in path info (Tomcat/Jetty defaults allow these; %2F/%5C and control bytes are the rejected cases). Victim user must follow the crafted link.
candidates.root_cause: ServiceListGeneratorServlet builds the stylesheet path for the formatted service list by concatenating request.getContextPath(), request.getServletPath() and request.getPathInfo() (the last is container-decoded attacker input) and passes it to FormattedServiceListWriter, which writes it verbatim into an HTML attribute: writer.write("<LINK type=\"text/css\" rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"" + styleSheetPath + "\">"). No HTML/attribute encoding or allow-list is applied to styleSheetPath (nor, in the same class, to the base path/endpoint addresses). Content type is text/html.
candidates.title: Reflected XSS in CXF service-list page via unencoded request path info written into HTML
candidates.trace: GET request -> AbstractHTTPServlet.handleRequest -> CXFServlet/CXFNonSpringServlet -> ServletController.invoke: pathInfo = request.getPathInfo(); if no destination matches and !isHideServiceList and (request.getRequestURI().endsWith("/services") || ... ), the full request is passed to ServiceListGeneratorServlet.service. There, with no service-list-stylesheet init param configured, styleSheetPath = contextPath + servletPath + pathInfo (+ "/" + "?stylesheet=1"); FormattedServiceListWriter.writeServiceList then emits "<LINK ... href=\"" + styleSheetPath + "\">" into a text/html response. A path ending in "/services" (to satisfy the routing check) whose earlier, percent-encoded segment contains HTML metacharacters therefore breaks out of the href attribute and executes script in the CXF origin.
candidates.unverified: No runtime/container test was executed (read-only review). The exact container acceptance of encoded <, >, " and space in path info was not verified in this environment, and the service-list vs destination routing outcome depends on the concrete endpoint layout. The snapshot is of unknown exact date (pom says 3.2.0-SNAPSHOT); no upstream patch/diff was consulted, so it is not established whether this corresponds to a particular CVE or whether later CXF releases added escaping.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Reflected XSS)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 4,762 files, 0 excluded by size/symlink/sensitive-name filters (binary-like files are refused/skipped by the read/search tools); notably all src/test sources are absent from the snapshot, so this review covers main/implementation sources only. P1 relation index: 4,762 files indexed, 0 source files missing from the index, 50,760 symbols, 151,626 call rows, 115,103 edges, 1,234 facts; index builds completed without running builds/tests and loaded no SAST or ground-truth findings, and its edges are syntactic navigation hints only. I inspected in depth: the servlet/HTTP transport path (CXFServlet, ServletController, ServiceListGeneratorServlet/FormattedServiceListWriter, DestinationRegistryImpl, AbstractHTTPServlet), attachment/MIME parsing (AttachmentDeserializer, MimeBodyPartInputStream, AttachmentSerializer, ContentDisposition, Rfc5987Util), XML parser hardening (StaxUtils, DOMUtils, Aegis/JAXB/WADL/XSLT parsers), JOSE/JWT and OAuth2/OIDC validation, SAML SSO response validation, WS-Security token/STS code, and TLS hostname-verification utilities. I did not exhaustively review the remaining modules (tools/, distribution/samples, CORBA/JMS/webservice/WS-* modules and most of the 2,353 rt files were only spot-checked or searched heuristically); no build, test, scanner, or runtime execution was performed.
limitations: No runtime confirmation: the XSS routing/decoding behavior was reasoned from source; no container (Tomcat/Jetty) or CXF deployment was executed.

The snapshot has no .git metadata and no tests, so the exact upstream revision/date and the corresponding fix are unknown; dependency versions (e.g., wss4j 2.1.5, Spring 4.2.6) and JAX-RS 2.1 features were used only as rough dating hints.

Container-dependent conditions (encoded metacharacters in path info, URI normalization, rejection of some encodings) and the endpoint layout (presence of a root '/' REST destination) can prevent or alter the service-list routing branch; these were not verified at runtime.
The P1 index provides syntactic call/containment/inheritance candidates only; I verified the cited edges against source text but did not perform exhaustive data-flow analysis over all 151k call rows.
Samples, tools, benchmark scripts, generated CORBA parser code, and several transport/security submodules were not line-by-line reviewed, so additional issues may exist there.

rejected_leads.lead: AttachmentDeserializer/MimeBodyPartInputStream unbounded MIME parsing (core/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/attachment/AttachmentDeserializer.java lines 314-368, MimeBodyPartInputStream.java): readLine/loadPartHeaders accumulate an unlimited number of arbitrary-length header lines and there is no cap on attachment count or header size, so a crafted multipart/related message to a JAX-WS MTOM/SwA or JAX-RS multipart endpoint could exhaust memory/CPU (DoS).
rejected_leads.reason: Real hardening gap and attacker-reachable on attachment-enabled endpoints, but impact is availability-only, requires a large request body, and no per-endpoint request-size limit in source proves exploitability. Kept as a secondary unconfirmed lead rather than the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuthJoseJwtConsumer.setDecryptWithClientSecret assigns the wrong field (rt/rs/security/oauth-parent/oauth2/.../OAuthJoseJwtConsumer.java lines 54-56: this.decryptWithClientSecret = verifyWithClientSecret) so JWE decryption with the client secret is not enabled as configured.
rejected_leads.reason: Unambiguous coding defect, but the setter is not used anywhere in this snapshot and the effect is mostly fail-closed (JwtException when decryption is needed) or a misconfiguration-dependent weakening of encryption enforcement; no source-evidenced token-acceptance bypass in default configurations.

rejected_leads.lead: OidcClaimsValidator.validateSelfIssuedProvider is an empty stub (rt/rs/security/sso/oidc/.../OidcClaimsValidator.java lines 115-116), so when supportSelfIssuedProvider is enabled and issuerId is unset, subject/audience/expiry checks are skipped for iss=https://self-issued.me tokens whose verification key is taken from the token's own sub_jwk claim.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the non-default supportSelfIssuedProvider flag; reachable impact not demonstrable from this snapshot alone and the self-issued flow is opt-in by design.

rejected_leads.lead: Unescaped HTML output in other components: AtomPullServer.addRecordToTable/startHtmlHeadAndBody (rt/management-web/.../AtomPullServer.java lines 502-530) writes log messages into HTML, and UndertowHTTPHandler.handleRequest (rt/transports/http-undertow/.../UndertowHTTPHandler.java lines 114-126) writes exception messages into an HTML error page.
rejected_leads.reason: Both are opt-in/secondary components (management log browser; Undertow transport needs a specific exception containing attacker-controlled text); weaker default reachability than the service-list page.

rejected_leads.lead: JwsUtils.loadSignatureVerifier accepts a JWK embedded in JWS headers (rt/rs/security/jose-parent/jose/.../JwsUtils.java lines 411-421) when the RSSEC_ACCEPT_PUBLIC_KEY message property is set.
rejected_leads.reason: Trusting the in-token key is the documented semantics of that opt-in property; default is false and throws, so this is not a source-evidenced vulnerability.

summary: Apache CXF 3.2.0-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (4,762 model-visible files, all test sources absent, no .git). After tracing request handling, attachment/MIME parsing, JOSE/OAuth2/OIDC, SAML SSO, WS-Security and TLS-client code, the single strongest source-evidenced candidate is a reflected XSS in the CXF servlet transport's default service-list page: the request-decoded path info is concatenated into the page's stylesheet href and written into an HTML response without any encoding. The same class also writes endpoint addresses/base path unescaped. Other plausible but weaker leads (unbounded MIME header/part parsing in AttachmentDeserializer, a wrong-field assignment in OAuthJoseJwtConsumer, an empty self-issued-provider validation in OidcClaimsValidator, unescaped HTML in the opt-in AtomPullServer/Undertow error page) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads. No candidate is runtime-confirmed; reachability of the XSS depends on container path handling and on the service-list page not being hidden.
